trap.title: Keratin or collagen?
trap.body: Keratin and collagen are both tough, fibrous structural proteins, so clues about strength and fibers can point either way. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body and fills tendons, ligaments, cartilage, bone, and the dermis, while keratin builds hair, nails, horns, feathers, and the outer layer of skin. Players also mix up keratin with chitin, the tough carbohydrate in insect and crab exoskeletons.
trap.fix: Hair, nails, horns, hooves, feathers, baleen, cysteine bridges, or perms mean keratin. Tendons, ligaments, a triple helix, or vitamin C mean collagen; insect exoskeletons or fungal cell walls mean chitin. Also check the noun: “this protein” is keratin, but “these cells” of the epidermis may want keratinocytes.
trap.line: Real answer line: Keratin (accept keratins, alpha-keratin, or beta-keratin; prompt on intermediate filaments; do not accept “collagen” or “chitin”)

topics.name: Leaves
topics.kicker: Plant organs that catch sunlight · Where most photosynthesis happens
topics.dates: Many change color in autumn as chlorophyll breaks down
topics.briefing: Leaves are a plant’s food factories: flat, green organs packed with chloroplasts that turn sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugar. Tiny pores called stomata on their surfaces let gases in and out, and veins bring in water and carry sugar away. In autumn, many trees break down the green chlorophyll in their leaves, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were hidden there all summer.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The arrangement of these structures on a stem, called phyllotaxis [“fil-uh-TAK-sis”], often forms spirals in which each new one sits about 137.5 degrees around the stem from the last, an angle linked to the Fibonacci numbers. Pairs of guard cells on these structures open and close tiny pores called stomata.
tossups.r: Their veins carry water and sugar. For 10 points, name these flat, green plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: In the Namib Desert, _Welwitschia_ [“wel-WITCH-ee-uh”] grows only two of these structures during its entire life, and they keep lengthening from their bases for centuries, splitting into ribbons. A waxy layer called the cuticle helps these structures avoid drying out.
tossups.r: Most are attached to stems by stalks called petioles. For 10 points, name these plant organs that carry out most photosynthesis.

tossups.p: In corn and other C4 plants, these structures have Kranz anatomy, named for the German word for “wreath,” because a ring of bundle-sheath cells surrounds each vein. In most plants, these structures have a middle layer called the mesophyll [“MEZ-uh-fil”].
tossups.r: Stomata on their surfaces let carbon dioxide in. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: As days grow shorter, many trees make red and purple pigments called anthocyanins [“an-thoh-SY-uh-ninz”] in these structures. A tree then seals off each of these structures with an abscission [“ab-SIZH-un”] layer at the base of its stalk so that it can drop off.
tossups.r: Their yellow and orange fall colors come from carotenoids that chlorophyll had hidden. For 10 points, name these plant organs that turn colors in autumn.

tossups.p: The bright red “petals” of a poinsettia [“poyn-SET-ee-uh”] are really bracts, colorful modified versions of these structures. Other modified versions of these structures include the spines of a cactus and the tendrils that pea plants use to climb.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs, usually flat and green, that are often attached to stems by stalks called petioles.

tossups.p: The sensitive plant, _Mimosa pudica_ [“mih-MOH-suh PYOO-dih-kuh”], folds up these structures within seconds of being touched, as water rushes out of cells at their bases. Venus flytraps catch insects with traps that are modified versions of these structures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs whose stomata let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis.

tossups.p: On cool, humid mornings, droplets of water can bead up along the edges of these structures after pushing out of pores called hydathodes [“HY-duh-thohdz”], a process called guttation. During the day, water evaporates from these structures in a process called transpiration.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these plant organs that are usually flat, green, and full of chloroplasts.

tossups.p: The crunchy stalks of celery are really the petioles [“PET-ee-ohlz”] of these structures, and rhubarb’s stalks are eaten too, even though the broad blades they hold contain poisonous oxalic acid. Tea is brewed from dried ones picked from a shrub called _Camellia sinensis_.
tossups.r: Their stomata let in carbon dioxide. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: The word “chlorophyll” combines a Greek word for “pale green” with the Greek word for these structures. Inside these structures, tall, tightly packed palisade cells lie above loosely packed spongy cells with air spaces between them.
tossups.r: Many of them turn yellow and orange in autumn. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: Silkworms feed on these structures from mulberry trees, monarch caterpillars eat those of milkweed plants, and koalas eat almost nothing but those of eucalyptus trees. Clover has compound ones, each divided into three smaller blades.
tossups.r: They are green because of chlorophyll. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

tossups.p: The layers of an onion bulb are thick, fleshy versions of these structures that store food underground. Pitcher plants trap insects in deep, slippery tubes that are also modified versions of these structures.
tossups.r: Most photosynthesis happens in them. For 10 points, name these plant organs whose stomata let gases in and out.

tossups.p: In many plants, most of the stomata on these structures are on their lower surface, which helps cut down on water loss. Each stoma is opened and closed by a pair of bean-shaped guard cells.
tossups.r: Water evaporating from these organs pulls more water up through the xylem. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: Grasses, corn, and other monocots usually have long, narrow versions of these structures with parallel veins, while eudicots such as oaks and maples have branching, net-like veins in them. Each vein is a vascular bundle with xylem on its upper side and phloem below.
tossups.r: Most photosynthesis happens inside them. For 10 points, name these plant organs that are green because of chlorophyll.

tossups.p: Horse chestnut trees have palmately compound versions of these structures, with blades spreading from one point like fingers, while ash trees have pinnately compound ones, with blades lined up along a central stalk like a feather. Poison ivy has compound ones with three blades.
tossups.r: A red one from a maple tree appears on Canada’s flag. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis happens.

tossups.p: In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz [“IN-gun-howss”] showed that plants give off oxygen only in sunlight, and only from their green parts, mainly these structures. The giant Amazon water lily has floating, round ones that can grow more than 2 meters across.
tossups.r: Deciduous trees drop theirs each fall. For 10 points, name these plant organs where most photosynthesis takes place.

clues.t: Flat, green plant organs where most photosynthesis happens, turning sunlight into sugar
Green because their cells are packed with chloroplasts full of chlorophyll
In autumn, many trees break down their chlorophyll, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids
Deciduous trees drop all of theirs each year; evergreens keep theirs year-round
A red one from a maple tree is on the flag of Canada
Pores called stomata, opened and closed by pairs of guard cells, let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapor out; in many plants, most are on the lower surface
Water evaporating from them (transpiration) pulls more water up through the xylem
Their middle layer, the mesophyll: tightly packed palisade cells on top, loosely packed spongy cells with air spaces below
A waxy cuticle on their outer surface helps keep them from drying out
Their veins are vascular bundles: xylem brings water in on the upper side, and phloem carries sugar out below
Monocots like grasses and corn have parallel veins; eudicots like oaks and maples have branching, net-like veins
Made of a flat blade and a stalk, called the petiole, that attaches it to the stem
Simple ones have a single blade; compound ones, like clover’s and poison ivy’s, are divided into several smaller blades
Cactus spines, pea tendrils, and the layers of an onion bulb are all modified versions
Silkworms eat mulberry ones, monarch caterpillars eat milkweed ones, and koalas eat eucalyptus ones
Their arrangement on a stem is called phyllotaxis; spirals often turn about 137.5 degrees (the golden angle) and follow Fibonacci numbers
_Welwitschia_ of the Namib Desert grows only two in its whole life; they keep growing from their bases for centuries
C4 plants like corn have Kranz (“wreath”) anatomy: a ring of bundle-sheath cells around each vein
In fall, many trees make red and purple anthocyanins in them, then seal each one off with an abscission layer at the base of its stalk
A poinsettia’s red “petals” are really bracts, a kind of modified one
The sensitive plant, _Mimosa pudica_, folds them up within seconds of being touched, as water rushes out of cells at their bases
The traps of Venus flytraps and the slippery tubes of pitcher plants are modified versions that catch insects
Guttation is the pushing of water droplets out of pores called hydathodes along their edges, often on humid mornings
Celery stalks are their petioles; rhubarb stalks are eaten but its blades hold poisonous oxalic acid; tea is brewed from dried ones
“Chlorophyll” joins Greek words for “pale green” and for this organ; the same root gives “phyllotaxis”
Horse chestnuts have palmately compound ones (blades spread like fingers); ash trees have pinnately compound ones (blades along a central stalk)
Jan Ingenhousz (1779) showed that plants give off oxygen only in sunlight and only from their green parts, mainly these organs
The giant Amazon water lily has floating, round ones that can grow more than 2 meters across

trap.title: Organ, not organelle
trap.body: Leaf tossups are full of photosynthesis clues, so players blurt the organelle (chloroplasts), the pigment (chlorophyll), the pores (stomata), or the process (photosynthesis) instead of the whole organ. Others answer “stems” for clues about modified leaves, like cactus spines, onion layers, or celery stalks, which don’t look like leaves at all.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “these organs” or “these structures” attached to stems by petioles means leaves. “This organelle” means chloroplasts, “these pores” means stomata, and “this pigment” means chlorophyll.
trap.line: Real answer line: Leaves (accept leaf or foliage; do not accept “chloroplasts” or “stomata”)

topics.name: Phloem
topics.kicker: Carries sugar from a plant’s leaves · Built from living sieve tubes
topics.briefing: Phloem is a plant’s food delivery system: living tubes that carry sugar made in the leaves to roots, fruits, flowers, and growing tips. Unlike xylem, which only moves water upward, phloem can carry its sugary sap up or down, wherever the plant needs food. Aphids tap into phloem to drink that sap, and peeling a ring of bark off a tree removes its phloem and can kill the tree by starving its roots.
topics.answerHtml: Phloem (prompt on vascular tissue or inner bark; do not accept “xylem”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli [“NAY-guh-lee”] named this tissue in 1858 from the Greek word for “bark,” and in trees it forms the inner bark. The vascular cambium adds new cells of this tissue toward the outside of a stem and new xylem toward the inside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves to the rest of a plant.

tossups.p: German botanist Ernst Münch proposed the pressure-flow hypothesis to explain how sap moves through this tissue. In that model, water drawn in by osmosis at a source, such as a leaf, builds up pressure that pushes the sap toward sinks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, unlike xylem, which carries water.

tossups.p: To collect pure samples of this tissue’s sap, scientists let an aphid feed, then cut its body away, leaving its needle-like stylet in place as a tiny tap. The sap in this tissue is under pressure, so it keeps flowing out of the cut stylet on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries sugar both up and down, unlike xylem.

tossups.p: When this tissue is wounded, its sieve plates are quickly plugged by a carbohydrate called callose [“KAL-ohs”] and by a protein called P-protein, which keep sap from leaking out. Its sieve-tube elements are stacked end to end to form long tubes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living vascular tissue that carries sugar made in the leaves.

tossups.p: In conifers, this tissue carries sap through sieve cells, which are helped by neighbors called Strasburger [“SHTRAHS-boor-ger”] cells or albuminous cells. Flowering plants instead use sieve-tube elements, each supported by a companion cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from leaves to the rest of the plant.

tossups.p: Mature sieve-tube elements in this tissue have no nucleus, so they depend on companion cells, which are linked to them by many tiny channels called plasmodesmata [“plaz-muh-dez-MAH-tuh”]. Each sieve-tube element is joined to the next by a perforated end wall called a sieve plate.
tossups.r: Companion cells also load sucrose into it. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries food made in the leaves.

tossups.p: Linen cloth is woven from the long, tough bast fibers of flax plants, which come from this tissue, and jute rope is made from similar fibers. In a tree, this tissue lies under the corky outer bark, forming the inner bark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, unlike the water-carrying xylem.

tossups.p: Citrus greening, a disease that has hurt orange groves in Florida, is caused by a bacterium that lives in this tissue and is spread by tiny insects called psyllids [“SIL-idz”]. Many plant viruses also spread through a plant by riding along in this tissue’s sap.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living plant tissue that carries sugar both up and down.

tossups.p: Larvae of the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle, kill ash trees by tunneling through this tissue and the cambium just under the bark. Girdling a tree, by cutting away a complete ring of bark, destroys this tissue all the way around the trunk.
tossups.r: The tree’s roots then starve. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves.

tossups.p: The flowering signal called florigen, which turned out to be a protein named FT, travels from the leaves to the tips of shoots through this tissue. In leaf veins, this tissue usually lies on the lower side, below the xylem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar, made of sieve tubes and companion cells.

tossups.p: Movement through this tissue, called translocation, carries sap from sources, such as mature leaves, to sinks, such as roots, fruits, and growing tips. A growing potato tuber is a sink that stores what it receives as starch.
tossups.r: Its sap can flow up or down. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar.

tossups.p: In many roots, strands of this tissue sit between the arms of an X-shaped core of xylem. In a typical stem, this tissue sits on the outer side of each vascular bundle, with xylem on the inner side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this living vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves to the rest of a plant.

tossups.p: Some ants guard aphids like herds of cattle and stroke them to collect honeydew, a sticky waste the aphids make from this tissue’s sap. Mosses and liverworts lack both this tissue and xylem, which helps keep them small.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tissue that carries sugar made in the leaves, unlike xylem, which carries water.

tossups.p: Cinnamon sticks are curls of the dried inner bark of certain tropical trees, a layer made mostly of this tissue. In a tree trunk, only a thin layer of this tissue next to the vascular cambium still carries sap; older layers are crushed outward into the bark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar both up and down a plant.

tossups.p: Companion cells are packed with mitochondria, since they spend ATP pumping sucrose into this tissue, a step called loading. Unloading at the other end lets fruits, seeds, and roots store what this tissue brings them.
tossups.r: Sugar beets and sugarcane store huge amounts of the sucrose it delivers. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries sugar from the leaves.

clues.t: Plant tissue that carries sugar (food) made in the leaves to the rest of the plant
One of the two vascular tissues, along with xylem, which carries water; mosses lack both
Its sap can flow up and down, while water in xylem moves only upward
Its conducting cells are alive when they work, unlike the dead, hollow cells of xylem
Sap flows through sieve-tube elements stacked end to end and joined by perforated walls called sieve plates
Mature sieve-tube elements have no nucleus, so neighboring companion cells keep them running
Moving sap through it is called translocation
Sap moves from sources, like mature leaves, to sinks, like roots, fruits, growing tips, and potato tubers
Carries sugar mainly as sucrose dissolved in water; sugar beets and sugarcane store huge amounts of it
Aphids drink its sap and release sticky honeydew, which some ants collect by guarding aphids like cattle
In trees it forms the inner bark; the vascular cambium adds it toward the outside and xylem toward the inside
Lies on the outer side of each vascular bundle in a stem, and on the lower side of leaf veins, below the xylem
Girdling, cutting away a ring of bark, destroys it all the way around and can kill a tree by starving its roots
Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli named it in 1858, from the Greek word for “bark”
Ernst Münch’s pressure-flow hypothesis: water drawn in by osmosis at a source builds pressure that pushes sap toward sinks
When it is wounded, sieve plates are plugged by a carbohydrate called callose and by P-protein
Scientists sample its sap by cutting away a feeding aphid and leaving its stylet in place; the sap flows out under pressure
Companion cells connect to sieve-tube elements through many tiny channels called plasmodesmata
Conifers use sieve cells helped by Strasburger (albuminous) cells instead of sieve tubes and companion cells
Its tough bast fibers give linen (from flax) and jute rope
Citrus greening, spread by tiny insects called psyllids, comes from a bacterium living in it; many plant viruses travel in its sap
Emerald ash borer larvae kill ash trees by tunneling through it and the cambium just under the bark
The flowering signal florigen, a protein named FT, travels through it from the leaves to the shoot tips
Companion cells, packed with mitochondria, spend ATP pumping sucrose into it, a step called loading
Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of certain trees, a layer made mostly of it; only its thin newest layer still carries sap
In many roots, its strands sit between the arms of an X-shaped core of xylem

trap.title: Phloem or xylem?
trap.body: Phloem and xylem are the two vascular tissues, and tossups often mention both. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves, in either direction, through living sieve-tube cells; xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots through dead, hollow cells. The vascular cambium, which makes new phloem and xylem, is a third answer players confuse with both.
trap.fix: Sugar, sucrose, sources and sinks, sieve tubes, companion cells, aphids, girdling, or the inner bark mean phloem. Water, minerals, transpiration, tracheids, vessel elements, wood, tree rings, or maple sap mean xylem. A memory trick: phloem carries food.
trap.line: Real answer line: Phloem (prompt on vascular tissue or inner bark; do not accept “xylem”)

topics.name: Lipids
topics.kicker: Fats, oils, waxes, and steroids · Store energy and build cell membranes
topics.briefing: Lipids are the greasy, water-fearing molecules of life: fats, oils, waxes, and steroids such as cholesterol. Because they are nonpolar, they don’t dissolve in water, which is why oil-and-vinegar salad dressing separates. Fats pack about 9 Calories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins, and phospholipids form the double layer that wraps every cell.
topics.answerHtml: Lipids (accept fats or lipid; prompt on triglycerides or oils; do not accept “fatty acids” or “carbohydrates”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the early 1800s, French chemist Michel Chevreul [“shuh-VRUHL”] showed that soap-making splits animal versions of these substances into glycerol and acids. That reaction, in which these substances are boiled with lye, is called saponification [“suh-pon-ih-fih-KAY-shun”].
tossups.r: They store about 9 Calories per gram. For 10 points, name this class of water-fearing biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and steroids.

tossups.p: Omega-3 molecules of this kind, found in fish such as salmon, have their first carbon-carbon double bond three carbons from the tail end of the chain. Linoleic [“lin-uh-LEE-ik”] acid, another one, is called “essential” because the body cannot make it and must get it from food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes triglycerides and steroids and does not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Lecithin [“LESS-ih-thin”] from egg yolks keeps mayonnaise from separating, since each of its molecules has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails. Molecules with that shape, one type of these substances, are called amphipathic [“am-fih-PATH-ik”].
tossups.r: That type forms the double layer of every cell membrane. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that also includes oils and waxes.

tossups.p: Bubbling hydrogen gas through liquid plant-based examples of these substances turns some of their carbon-carbon double bonds into single bonds, making solid spreads like margarine. That partial hydrogenation also creates “trans” versions of these molecules, which are linked to heart disease.
tossups.r: Saturated ones, like butter, have no double bonds and are solid at room temperature. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that include triglycerides.

tossups.p: In the emulsion test for these substances, a food sample is shaken with ethanol and then poured into water, where these substances turn the mixture cloudy white. The dye Sudan III [“soo-DAN three”] stains these substances red.
tossups.r: Rubbing them on brown paper leaves a see-through spot. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that include oils and waxes.

tossups.p: After digestion, these molecules are packed into particles called chylomicrons [“kye-loh-MY-kronz”] and absorbed into lacteals, tiny lymph vessels inside the villi of the small intestine. Before that, bile salts help gather them into tiny clusters called micelles [“my-SELZ”].
tossups.r: Enzymes called lipases break them down. For 10 points, name these energy-rich biomolecules that do not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Brown adipose tissue burns stored molecules of this kind to make heat instead of ATP, using a protein called thermogenin inside its mitochondria. White adipose tissue stores these molecules and also cushions organs and insulates the body.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these biomolecules, including triglycerides, that store about 9 Calories of energy per gram.

tossups.p: Three ester bonds form when a glycerol molecule joins three long acid chains in a dehydration synthesis that releases three molecules of water. The molecule built that way, a triglyceride [“try-GLISS-er-ide”], is the most common kind of these substances in food.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and steroids such as cholesterol.

tossups.p: The myelin sheaths that insulate nerve fibers are made mostly of these substances, which is one reason the brain is so rich in them. One group of these substances, which includes testosterone and estrogen, is built from four fused carbon rings.
tossups.r: That group, the steroids, includes cholesterol. For 10 points, name this class of water-fearing biomolecules.

tossups.p: Cells that make large amounts of these substances, such as those in the adrenal glands, are packed with smooth endoplasmic reticulum, the organelle that builds them. Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in these substances rather than in water, so the body can store them.
tossups.r: They do not mix with water. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils, waxes, and cholesterol.

tossups.p: When food rich in these substances reaches the small intestine, the gut releases cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], which makes the gallbladder squeeze out bile. Bile then breaks these substances into tiny droplets so enzymes can reach them, a process called emulsification.
tossups.r: Pancreatic lipase then breaks them into fatty acids and glycerol. For 10 points, name these biomolecules that do not dissolve in water.

tossups.p: Chips and nuts go rancid when oxygen attacks the double bonds in these molecules, so companies add antioxidants such as vitamin E to slow the damage. Unsaturated versions of these molecules have kinks at those double bonds, which keep them liquid at room temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules, including oils and waxes, that stores long-term energy.

tossups.p: A camel’s hump is not a water tank but a store of these substances, which the camel can break down for energy when food is scarce. Whales and seals stay warm in icy water thanks to blubber, a thick layer of these substances under the skin.
tossups.r: Butter and olive oil are rich in them. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes triglycerides, oils, and waxes.

tossups.p: Soap cleans greasy dishes because each soap molecule has a long nonpolar tail that dissolves in these substances and a charged head that dissolves in water. Bile salts work in a similar way, coating tiny droplets of these substances in the small intestine.
tossups.r: These substances are nonpolar, so they don’t mix with water. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules.

tossups.p: Fish that live in icy water build their cell membranes with extra unsaturated molecules of this kind, whose kinked tails keep the membranes from stiffening in the cold. Saturated molecules of this kind have straight tails that pack tightly together.
tossups.r: That is why butter is solid at room temperature. For 10 points, name this class of biomolecules that includes oils and waxes.

clues.t: Biomolecules that do not dissolve in water because they are nonpolar (hydrophobic, or “water-fearing”)
Include oils, waxes, and steroids such as cholesterol
Store energy: about 9 Calories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins
Molecules with a phosphate head and two tails form the double layer (bilayer) of every cell membrane
One of the four main kinds of biomolecules, along with carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids
Triglycerides: three fatty acids attached to one glycerol, the most common kind in food
Saturated ones have no carbon-carbon double bonds and are solid at room temperature, like butter; unsaturated ones have kinks and stay liquid
Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, breaks them into tiny droplets (emulsification)
Enzymes called lipases, mostly from the pancreas, break them into fatty acids and glycerol
Food tests: Sudan III dye stains them red, and they leave a see-through grease spot on brown paper
Built by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which is plentiful in cells like those of the adrenal glands
Stored in adipose tissue, which cushions organs and insulates the body; whale blubber and camel humps are big stores of them
Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in them instead of in water, so the body can store those vitamins
Waxes, like beeswax and the cuticle that coats leaves, keep water out
Steroids, such as cholesterol, testosterone, and estrogen, are built from four fused carbon rings
Glycerol joins its three acid chains by ester bonds in a dehydration synthesis that releases water
Hydrogenation turns liquid plant oils into solid spreads like margarine; partial hydrogenation creates “trans” versions linked to heart disease
Omega-3 ones (in fish like salmon) have their first double bond three carbons from the tail end; linoleic acid is “essential,” so it must come from food
Michel Chevreul showed in the early 1800s that soap-making splits animal ones into glycerol and acids
Boiling them with lye, a strong base, makes soap and glycerol, a reaction called saponification
Emulsion test: shake a sample with ethanol, pour it into water, and these turn the mixture cloudy white
Bile salts gather them into micelles; then they are packed into chylomicrons and absorbed by lacteals in the villi
Lecithin from egg yolks keeps mayonnaise from separating; its molecules are amphipathic, with a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails
Brown adipose tissue burns them to make heat, using thermogenin in its mitochondria
Myelin sheaths around nerve fibers are made mostly of them, so the brain is rich in them
Soap cleans grease because each soap molecule has a nonpolar tail that dissolves in these and a charged head that dissolves in water
They go rancid when oxygen attacks their double bonds, so antioxidants such as vitamin E are added to foods
Fish in icy water put extra unsaturated ones in their cell membranes, since kinked tails keep membranes from stiffening

trap.title: The family, not one member
trap.body: Lipid tossups name many family members, such as triglycerides, phospholipids, cholesterol, and waxes, and many parts, such as fatty acids and glycerol, so players blurt one of those instead of the whole class. “Triglycerides” or “oils” earns only a prompt, and “fatty acids” is wrong because fatty acids are just building blocks. Players also confuse lipids with carbohydrates, since both store energy and are made mostly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the whole class, including steroids, waxes, or membrane molecules, say “lipids” (or “fats”). Water-fearing, nonpolar, 9 Calories per gram, Sudan III, or bile mean lipids; sugars, starch, 4 Calories per gram, or Benedict’s and iodine tests mean carbohydrates.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lipids (accept fats or lipid; prompt on triglycerides or oils; do not accept “fatty acids” or “carbohydrates”)

topics.name: Marsupials
topics.kicker: Pouched mammals like kangaroos and koalas · Most live in Australia
topics.dates: The Virginia opossum is the only one north of Mexico
topics.briefing: Marsupials are mammals that give birth to tiny, underdeveloped babies, which usually keep growing inside the mother’s pouch. A newborn red kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean, yet it crawls into the pouch on its own and stays there for months as a “joey.” Most marsupials, including kangaroos, koalas, wombats, and Tasmanian devils, live in Australia and New Guinea, but opossums live in the Americas.
topics.answerHtml: Marsupials (accept Marsupialia, metatherians, or pouched mammals; prompt on mammals; do not accept “monotremes” or “placental mammals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The largest member of this group ever, _Diprotodon_ [“dye-PROH-tuh-don”], was a rhinoceros-sized plant-eater that died out tens of thousands of years ago. Fossils show that members of this group once lived in Antarctica, which linked South America to Australia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: In 1770, members of James Cook’s expedition wrote down the Guugu Yimithirr [“GOO-goo YIM-ih-theer”] word gangurru, which became the English name for some of these animals. Members of this group called macropods, a name meaning “big foot,” hop on long hind feet.
tossups.r: Those animals are kangaroos. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies, called joeys, usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: An island near Perth got the name Rottnest, meaning “rat’s nest,” after a Dutch explorer mistook its quokkas [“KWOK-uhz”], small members of this group, for giant rats. The numbat, another member of this group, eats almost nothing but termites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos, koalas, and wombats, that usually carry their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: The monito del monte [“moh-NEE-toh del MON-tay”], a tiny member of this group from the forests of Chile and Argentina, is more closely related to members on another continent than to the opossums living around it. Shrew opossums form another South American branch of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The last known thylacine [“THY-luh-seen”], a striped, dog-like meat-eater of this group nicknamed the Tasmanian tiger, died in a zoo in Hobart in 1936. Because thylacines looked so much like wolves without being closely related, they are a classic example of convergent evolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including the Tasmanian devil and the koala, that usually raise their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: One member of this group has fingerprints so similar to human ones that they can be hard to tell apart under a microscope. That animal eats almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves and sleeps up to about 20 hours a day.
tossups.r: That animal is the koala, which is not a bear. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: At Easter, some stores sell chocolate bilbies instead of bunnies to help protect the bilby, a big-eared, burrowing member of this group. The sugar glider, another member of this group, glides between trees on flaps of skin stretched between its front and back legs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including wombats and kangaroos, whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The only member of this group native to the United States and Canada has 50 teeth, a prehensile tail, and thumb-like big toes on its hind feet. When threatened, that animal may “play possum,” going limp and pretending to be dead.
tossups.r: That animal is the Virginia opossum. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose young usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: Wild populations of the largest living meat-eating member of this group have shrunk because of devil facial tumor disease, a contagious cancer that spreads between animals when they bite each other. The Looney Tunes cartoon character Taz is based on that animal.
tossups.r: That animal is the Tasmanian devil. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, whose newborns crawl into a pouch.

tossups.p: When grazing slowly, the biggest living members of this group lean on their thick, muscular tails as a fifth leg, a gait called pentapedal [“pen-tuh-PEE-dul”] locomotion. At higher speeds, springy tendons in their long hind legs store energy with each hop.
tossups.r: Those animals are red kangaroos. For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies are called joeys.

tossups.p: One burrowing member of this group leaves cube-shaped droppings, which it piles on rocks and logs to mark its territory, and scientists who studied how it makes those cubes won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize. Its teeth never stop growing, much like a rodent’s front teeth.
tossups.r: That animal is the wombat, whose pouch faces backward. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos.

tossups.p: Crash, the hero of a video game series that began in 1996, is a bandicoot, a long-snouted member of this group. Kanga and her son Roo, characters in A. A. Milne’s stories about Winnie-the-Pooh, are also members of this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals whose babies, called joeys, usually grow in a pouch.

tossups.p: The honey possum, a mouse-sized member of this group, is one of the few mammals that feed only on nectar and pollen, which it laps up with a long, brush-tipped tongue. The possums of Australia and the opossums of the Americas are different animals, but both belong to this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos and koalas, that usually raise their young in a pouch.

tossups.p: Members of this group have a pair of epipubic [“ep-ih-PYOO-bik”] bones that jut forward from the hips, a feature they share with the egg-laying monotremes. Unlike monotremes, members of this group give birth to live young after a very short pregnancy, often lasting only a few weeks.
tossups.r: Their tiny newborns crawl into a pouch. For 10 points, name this group of mammals.

tossups.p: Many members of this group can put an early embryo on hold for months, a process called embryonic diapause [“DY-uh-pawz”], so that a new baby develops only when the timing is right. The newborn of the largest living member of this group is only about the size of a jellybean.
tossups.r: Those newborns crawl into the mother’s pouch on their own. For 10 points, name this group of mammals, including kangaroos.

clues.t: Mammals whose tiny, underdeveloped newborns usually keep growing in the mother’s pouch
Kangaroos, koalas, and wombats are examples
Most live in Australia and New Guinea
Their babies are called joeys
One of the three living groups of mammals, with the egg-laying monotremes and the placental mammals
The Virginia opossum is the only one native to the U.S. and Canada; it may “play possum,” pretending to be dead
The Virginia opossum has 50 teeth, a prehensile tail, and thumb-like big toes on its hind feet
Koalas eat almost only eucalyptus leaves, sleep up to about 20 hours a day, and are not bears
The Tasmanian devil, the largest living meat-eating one, survives in the wild mainly on Tasmania; Looney Tunes’ Taz is based on it
The red kangaroo is the largest living one; its newborn is about the size of a jellybean after a pregnancy of only weeks
Wombats dig burrows, have backward-facing pouches, and leave cube-shaped droppings
Sugar gliders glide on skin flaps between their front and back legs, like unrelated flying squirrels
Kangaroos and wallabies are macropods, a name meaning “big foot”
The possums of Australia and the opossums of the Americas are different animals, but both are in this group
_Diprotodon_, a rhinoceros-sized plant-eater that died out tens of thousands of years ago, was the largest one ever
Fossils show they lived in Antarctica when it linked South America and Australia; Chile’s monito del monte is closer kin to Australian ones than to nearby opossums
“Kangaroo” comes from gangurru in the Guugu Yimithirr language, written down by James Cook’s expedition in 1770
Rottnest Island (“rat’s nest”) near Perth was named when a Dutch explorer mistook its quokkas for rats; striped numbats eat termites
The last known thylacine (Tasmanian tiger) died in a Hobart zoo in 1936; it looked like a wolf without being related, a case of convergent evolution
Koala fingerprints are so similar to human ones that they can be hard to tell apart
Chocolate bilbies are sold at Easter instead of bunnies to help protect the big-eared bilby
Devil facial tumor disease, a contagious cancer spread by bites, has shrunk wild Tasmanian devil populations
Kangaroos lean on their tails as a fifth leg when moving slowly (pentapedal locomotion); springy tendons store energy when they hop
Scientists who studied how wombats make cube-shaped droppings won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize; wombat teeth never stop growing
Crash, a video game hero since 1996, is a bandicoot; Kanga and Roo from the Winnie-the-Pooh stories are kangaroos
The mouse-sized honey possum feeds only on nectar and pollen, using a long, brush-tipped tongue
They have epipubic bones jutting forward from the hips, a feature shared with monotremes
Many can put an early embryo on hold for months, a process called embryonic diapause

trap.title: Pouches versus eggs
trap.body: Australia is also home to the platypus and the echidnas, which are monotremes: mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to tiny young. Some look-alikes and sound-alikes are actually placental mammals, such as kangaroo rats (rodents) and flying squirrels, and the koala “bear” is not a bear at all. Answering a single animal, like “kangaroos,” loses a tossup that asks for the whole group.
trap.fix: Pouches, joeys, opossums, epipubic bones, or tiny newborns that crawl to the pouch mean marsupials. Eggs, the platypus, or echidnas mean monotremes, and a long pregnancy fed by a long-lasting placenta means placental mammals. If the question says “this group” or “these mammals,” give the group name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Marsupials (accept Marsupialia, metatherians, or pouched mammals; prompt on mammals; do not accept “monotremes” or “placental mammals”)

topics.name: Metamorphosis
topics.kicker: Change from larva to adult form · Caterpillar to butterfly, tadpole to frog
topics.dates: Seen in insects, amphibians, and many sea animals
topics.briefing: A caterpillar seals itself inside a chrysalis, breaks down much of its own body, and comes out days or weeks later as a butterfly. That dramatic change in body form is metamorphosis, from Greek words meaning “change of shape.” Frogs do it too: a tadpole grows legs and lungs and absorbs its tail, a switch set off by thyroid hormone, while insects rely on hormones called ecdysone and juvenile hormone.
topics.answerHtml: Metamorphosis (accept complete or incomplete metamorphosis; prompt on development or life cycle; do not accept “molting” or “ecdysis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Pockets of cells called imaginal discs sit inside a larva until this process, when they develop into wings, legs, and eyes. Much of the larva’s old body breaks down during this process, and the adult finally climbs out in a step called eclosion [“ih-KLOH-zhun”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which an animal changes body form, as when a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.

tossups.p: When an insect’s level of juvenile hormone drops, its next molt begins this process instead of producing a bigger larva. The steroid hormone ecdysone [“EK-dih-sohn”] triggers each of those molts, which separate growth stages called instars.
tossups.r: In butterflies, this process passes through a pupa called a chrysalis. For 10 points, name this change in body form from larva to adult.

tossups.p: During this process, an animal switches from getting rid of its waste as ammonia to making urea, and its long, coiled gut, built for digesting plants, gets much shorter. Thyroid hormone controls this process, which also makes the animal’s tail shrink away through programmed cell death.
tossups.r: The animal’s hind legs appear first, then its front legs. For 10 points, name this process in which a tadpole becomes a frog.

tossups.p: The axolotl [“AK-suh-lot-ul”], a Mexican salamander, normally does not go through this process and keeps its feathery outside gills as an adult. Scientists can still push an axolotl through this process by giving it thyroid hormone.
tossups.r: Frogs go through this process as they lose their gills and tails. For 10 points, name this dramatic change in body form, from larva to adult.

tossups.p: In 1705, the German-born artist Maria Sibylla Merian [“MAIR-ee-un”] published paintings of insects she had studied in Suriname, showing every stage of this process beside the plants the insects ate. In the 1600s, the Dutch scientist Jan Swammerdam dissected insects to show that all the stages of this process belong to one animal.
tossups.r: In butterflies, its resting stage takes place inside a chrysalis. For 10 points, name this process in which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.

tossups.p: Mayflies are the only living insects that molt again after they already have working wings, passing through a winged stage called the subimago. Dragonflies follow a three-stage form of this process, in which underwater nymphs called naiads [“NYE-adz”] crawl out of the water for one last molt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of changing body form, which butterflies complete in four stages.

tossups.p: A young flounder goes through this process when one of its eyes slowly moves across its head to join the other eye, so the fish can lie flat on the seafloor. Lampreys spend years as filter-feeding larvae called ammocoetes [“AM-uh-seets”] before this process gives them their adult form.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this change in body form that also turns a tadpole into a frog.

tossups.p: Puerto Rico’s coquí [“koh-KEE”] frogs skip the free-swimming larval stage that usually comes before this process: their eggs hatch straight into tiny froglets. In most frogs, the back legs appear during this process before the front legs.
tossups.r: The tail and gills then disappear. For 10 points, name this process in which a tadpole changes into an adult frog.

tossups.p: Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground as nymphs before climbing a tree for the final molt of their three-stage form of this process, leaving their empty shells behind. Grasshoppers and cockroaches also follow that “incomplete” form of this process, which has no pupa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of changing body form, which a caterpillar finishes inside a chrysalis.

tossups.p: Silverfish never go through this process, since their young already look like small adults. In the “complete” form of this process, a larva molts several times, then rests as a pupa before emerging as an adult, or imago [“ih-MAY-goh”].
tossups.r: Its name comes from Greek words for “change of shape.” For 10 points, name this process that turns caterpillars into butterflies.

tossups.p: In 1912, J. F. Gudernatsch [“GOO-der-nahch”] found that young amphibians fed thyroid tissue began this process early, evidence that the thyroid gland controls it. During this process, gills disappear as lungs take over, and the tail is absorbed through programmed cell death, or apoptosis.
tossups.r: Back legs appear before front legs during this process. For 10 points, name this process that turns a tadpole into a frog.

tossups.p: Right after this process ends with eclosion, a newly emerged insect pumps fluid into the veins of its crumpled wings to stretch them out. Before that, a monarch spends the resting stage of this process inside a jade-green case dotted with gold.
tossups.r: That case is a chrysalis. For 10 points, name this process in which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.

tossups.p: Mosquito larvae, nicknamed “wrigglers,” and comma-shaped mosquito pupae, nicknamed “tumblers,” both live in water before this process ends with a flying adult. Fly larvae called maggots and beetle larvae called grubs also go through the four-stage form of this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that changes a caterpillar into a butterfly or a tadpole into a frog.

tossups.p: Sea squirts begin life as swimming larvae with a tail and a stiff rod called a notochord, then glue themselves to a rock and absorb that tail during this process. Sea star larvae have two matching halves until this process gives them five-part radial symmetry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process of dramatic body change, which also turns caterpillars into butterflies.

tossups.p: The silk used to weave fine cloth is unwound from the cases that silkworms spin around themselves during this process. Many other moths also spend the resting pupa stage of this process inside a silk cocoon.
tossups.r: Butterflies instead form a hard case called a chrysalis. For 10 points, name this process that turns a caterpillar into a winged adult.

clues.t: The classic example: a caterpillar turning into a butterfly
A tadpole changing into a frog, growing legs and lungs and losing its tail
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “change of shape”
The “complete” form has four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult, as in butterflies, beetles, and flies
The “incomplete” form has three stages, egg, nymph, and adult, with no pupa, as in grasshoppers
A butterfly pupa is a hard chrysalis; many moth pupae rest inside a silk cocoon, and silkworm cocoons give us silk
Larvae with special names: caterpillars (butterflies and moths), maggots (flies), and grubs (beetles)
In insects, the steroid hormone ecdysone triggers each molt
Juvenile hormone keeps an insect a larva; when its level drops, the next molt makes a pupa or adult
In frogs and other amphibians, thyroid hormone sets it off
A tadpole’s tail is absorbed through apoptosis, or programmed cell death
Tadpoles breathe with gills; adult frogs breathe with lungs and through their skin; back legs appear before front legs
The stages between a larva’s molts are called instars; the final adult stage is the imago
Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and rest in a jade-green chrysalis dotted with gold
Periodical cicadas live underground as nymphs for 13 or 17 years before their final molt
Imaginal discs, pockets of cells in a larva, grow into adult wings, legs, and eyes during the pupa stage
The adult’s emergence from the pupa is called eclosion; a butterfly then pumps fluid into its wing veins to spread its wings
The axolotl, a Mexican salamander, normally skips it and keeps its gills as an adult, but thyroid hormone can force the change
Tadpoles get rid of waste as ammonia, but adult frogs make urea; the tadpole’s long, coiled, plant-digesting gut shortens
In 1912, J. F. Gudernatsch fed thyroid tissue to young amphibians, and they changed early
Maria Sibylla Merian painted insect life cycles from Suriname, with the plants they ate, in a 1705 book
In the 1600s, Dutch scientist Jan Swammerdam dissected insects to show that larva, pupa, and adult are one animal
Silverfish never go through it: their young already look like small adults
Dragonfly and mayfly nymphs, called naiads, live underwater; mayflies are the only living insects that molt again after getting working wings (the subimago)
In young flounders and other flatfish, one eye moves across the head to join the other
Lamprey larvae, called ammocoetes, filter-feed in stream beds for years before changing into adults
Puerto Rico’s coquí frogs skip the swimming larva: their eggs hatch straight into tiny froglets
Sea squirt larvae lose their tails and notochords after settling on rocks; sea star larvae change from two-sided to five-part symmetry

trap.title: Biology, not Kafka
trap.body: Literature has two answer lines with nearly the same name: Franz Kafka’s novella _The Metamorphosis_, in which Gregor Samsa wakes up turned into a giant insect, and Ovid’s Latin poem _Metamorphoses_, a collection of myths about transformations. In science, players also confuse this process with molting, the shedding of an exoskeleton, which happens many times as an insect grows.
trap.fix: “This novella” or Gregor Samsa means Kafka’s book; “this poem” or Ovid means _Metamorphoses_. “This process” with larvae, pupae, tadpoles, or hormones means the biology answer. Molting (ecdysis) is only one step along the way, so don’t say it when the question asks for the whole change in body form.
trap.line: Real answer line: Metamorphosis (accept complete or incomplete metamorphosis; do not accept “molting”)

topics.name: Nucleotides
topics.kicker: Building blocks of DNA and RNA · A sugar, a phosphate, and a base
topics.dates: About 3 billion pairs in one copy of the human genome
topics.briefing: Every strand of DNA and RNA is a chain of nucleotides, small units that each join a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group to a nitrogen-containing base. DNA’s four bases, adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine, are the four “letters” of the genetic code, and RNA swaps thymine for uracil. Nucleotides have other jobs too: ATP, the molecule cells spend for energy, is one of them.
topics.answerHtml: Nucleotides (accept nucleotide, deoxyribonucleotides, or ribonucleotides; prompt on bases or nitrogenous bases; do not accept “nucleosides” or “nucleic acids”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Albrecht Kossel won the 1910 Nobel Prize in medicine for work on cell chemistry that included identifying the bases in these molecules. Each of these molecules has a nitrogen-containing base attached to the first carbon of a five-carbon sugar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA and RNA, each made of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base.

tossups.p: Phoebus Levene [“luh-VEEN”] wrongly proposed that DNA was a dull chain of the same four of these units repeated over and over, which made it seem too simple to carry genes. Erwin Chargaff helped disprove that idea by showing that DNA from different species contains these units in different amounts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these units, each containing a base like adenine or guanine, that link up to form nucleic acids.

tossups.p: Frederick Sanger’s method for reading DNA used special versions of these molecules that lack the hydroxyl group on the sugar’s three-prime carbon, so a growing strand stops wherever one is added. Normally, the enzyme DNA polymerase adds each new one of these molecules to the three-prime end of a strand.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules that join to form DNA and RNA, each made of a sugar, a phosphate, and a base.

tossups.p: Phosphodiester [“FOSS-foh-dye-ESS-ter”] bonds link these molecules, joining the three-prime carbon of one sugar to the phosphate on the five-prime carbon of the next. A chain of these molecules therefore has a “backbone” of alternating sugars and phosphates, with bases sticking out to the side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these monomers that link up to form nucleic acids such as DNA.

tossups.p: These molecules are sorted by whether their bases are double-ringed purines [“PYOOR-eenz”] or single-ringed pyrimidines [“pih-RIM-ih-deenz”]. In the double helix, one of these molecules containing guanine pairs with one containing cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, while adenine and thymine share two.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA, each made of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.

tossups.p: Earl Sutherland won a Nobel Prize for his work on cyclic AMP, a ring-shaped one of these molecules that relays hormone signals inside cells. The electron carrier NAD+ is made of two of these molecules joined through their phosphate groups.
tossups.r: The energy carrier ATP is another one of them. For 10 points, name these molecules that are also the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

tossups.p: When DNA is copied, the lagging strand is built in short runs of these units called Okazaki [“oh-kah-ZAH-kee”] fragments, which DNA ligase then seals together. A new strand grows only at its three-prime end, where the next one of these units attaches to a free hydroxyl group on the last sugar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA, which come in four kinds labeled A, C, G, and T.

tossups.p: Human telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, repeat the same six of these units, TTAGGG, over and over. Genetic differences called SNPs [“snips”] are spots where people’s DNA differs at just one of these units.
tossups.r: A point mutation changes just one of them. For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA and RNA.

tossups.p: When the body breaks down the purine bases from these molecules, it makes uric acid, which can build up into the crystals that cause gout. Without its phosphate group, one of these molecules is called a nucleoside [“NOO-klee-oh-side”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these units, each with a sugar, a phosphate, and a base, that are linked together to make DNA.

tossups.p: Arthur Kornberg shared the 1959 Nobel Prize for finding a bacterial enzyme that links these units into DNA, while Severo Ochoa [“oh-CHOH-uh”] shared it for an enzyme that links them into RNA. The raw materials DNA polymerase uses carry three phosphate groups, two of which break off as each unit joins the chain.
tossups.r: Phosphodiester bonds then hold the units together in a sugar-phosphate backbone. For 10 points, name these building blocks of nucleic acids.

tossups.p: The sugar in the DNA version of these molecules is missing one oxygen atom on its second carbon, which is why it is called deoxyribose. In the RNA version of these molecules, the sugar is ribose, and the base uracil takes the place of thymine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these units, each made of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base, that form DNA and RNA.

tossups.p: Cells can switch genes off by attaching methyl groups to the cytosine-containing versions of these molecules in DNA. A frameshift mutation happens when one or two of these units are added or removed, which throws off how a gene is read in groups of three.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA, each made of a sugar, a phosphate, and a base.

tossups.p: In these molecules, the base is joined to the sugar’s one-prime carbon by a glycosidic [“gly-koh-SID-ik”] bond, while the phosphate hangs off the five-prime carbon. The sugar’s carbons are numbered with prime marks to tell them apart from the atoms in the base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these units whose bases pair up to form the rungs of the DNA ladder.

tossups.p: A polymerase chain reaction tube holds short primers, a heat-resistant enzyme called Taq polymerase, and a supply of these molecules, which the enzyme strings together to make many copies of a stretch of DNA. One copy of the human genome contains about three billion pairs of these units.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of DNA, each with a sugar, a phosphate, and a base.

tossups.p: Chargaff’s rules say that in DNA, the number of these units containing adenine equals the number containing thymine. Messenger RNA is read three of these units at a time, and most of those triplets, called codons, stand for one amino acid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, each made of a sugar, a phosphate, and a base, that link up to form DNA and RNA.

G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs by two
ATP, the cell’s main energy carrier, is one, with three phosphate groups

Chargaff’s rules: in DNA, the amount with adenine equals the amount with thymine, and guanine equals cytosine
DNA polymerase adds each new one to the three-prime end of a growing strand
Albrecht Kossel, who identified the bases found in them, won the 1910 Nobel Prize in medicine
Phoebus Levene wrongly thought DNA was a dull repeat of the same four of them; Chargaff helped disprove it
Frederick Sanger’s DNA-reading method used versions missing the three-prime hydroxyl group, which stop a growing strand
Arthur Kornberg and Severo Ochoa shared the 1959 Nobel Prize for enzymes that link them into DNA and RNA
They join a chain as triphosphates, and two of the three phosphates break off as each one is added
Cyclic AMP, a ring-shaped one, relays hormone signals (Earl Sutherland, Nobel Prize); NAD+ is two of them joined together
The lagging strand is built in short runs called Okazaki fragments, sealed together by DNA ligase
The base joins the sugar’s one-prime carbon by a glycosidic bond; the phosphate sits on the five-prime carbon
Breaking down their purine bases makes uric acid, which can build up and cause gout
Human telomeres repeat the six-unit sequence TTAGGG over and over

trap.title: Nucleotide, nucleoside, or base?
trap.body: Four answer lines sound alike. A nucleotide has three parts: sugar, phosphate, and base. A nucleoside is only the sugar and base, with no phosphate, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are the long chains that nucleotides build. The bases (adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine, uracil) are just one part, and some tossups ask for one of them, like uracil, by name.
trap.fix: Count the parts. A sugar, a phosphate, and a base, or “these monomers,” means nucleotides; no phosphate means nucleoside; “this polymer” or a double helix means a nucleic acid. Saying only “bases” earns a prompt, so be ready to say “nucleotides.” Don’t mix them up with amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
trap.line: Real answer line: Nucleotides (prompt on bases; do not accept “nucleosides” or “nucleic acids”)

topics.name: Penicillin
topics.kicker: Antibiotic Alexander Fleming found in a mold · Fights bacterial infections
topics.briefing: In 1928, Alexander Fleming came back from a summer vacation to his London lab and found a mold growing on one of his dishes of bacteria, with a clear, germ-free ring around it. The mold was making penicillin, which kills bacteria by stopping them from building their cell walls. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain later turned it into a real medicine, and it saved huge numbers of lives during World War II.
topics.answerHtml: Penicillin (accept penicillin G, penicillin V, or benzylpenicillin; prompt on antibiotics or beta-lactam antibiotics; do not accept “Penicillium” or “amoxicillin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A lab worker nicknamed “Moldy Mary” found an especially productive strain of the mold that makes this drug on a cantaloupe from a market in Peoria, Illinois. Scientists at a government lab in Peoria boosted production of this drug by growing that mold in deep tanks fed with corn steep liquor.
tossups.r: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain had already turned this drug into a medicine at Oxford. For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.

tossups.p: In 1945, Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin used X-ray crystallography to show that this drug contains a strained, four-membered ring called a beta-lactam [“BAY-tuh LAK-tam”] ring. Hodgkin later won the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for finding the structures of molecules, including this drug and vitamin B12.
tossups.r: It kills bacteria by blocking how they build their cell walls. For 10 points, name this antibiotic made by a mold, which Alexander Fleming discovered.

tossups.p: This drug binds to enzymes called transpeptidases [“trans-PEP-tih-day-sez”] and stops them from cross-linking peptidoglycan [“pep-tih-doh-GLY-kan”], so a growing bacterium’s wall turns weak and the cell bursts. Human cells are not harmed by this drug because they have no cell walls.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antibiotic that Alexander Fleming discovered when a mold killed bacteria in one of his dishes.

tossups.p: Some bacteria resist this drug by making beta-lactamase [“BAY-tuh LAK-tuh-mayss”] enzymes that break open its four-membered ring, which is why its relative amoxicillin is often combined with clavulanic [“klav-yoo-LAN-ik”] acid, a chemical that blocks those enzymes. MRSA is a staph bacterium that resists another relative of this drug, methicillin.
tossups.r: It was mass-produced for Allied troops during World War II. For 10 points, name this antibiotic produced by a mold and discovered by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: Norman Heatley worked out how to extract this drug from mold broth at Oxford, where his team grew the mold in shallow containers that included hospital bedpans. Their team, led by Howard Florey with Ernst Chain, showed in 1940 that this drug could protect infected mice.
tossups.r: Florey, Chain, and Alexander Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for this drug. For 10 points, name this antibiotic made by a mold.

tossups.p: In 1942, Anne Miller of New Haven, Connecticut, became one of the first patients in the United States to be treated successfully with this drug. By the D-Day invasion in 1944, American factories were making enough of this drug to treat wounded Allied soldiers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antibiotic, which Alexander Fleming first noticed when a mold killed bacteria on one of his dishes.

tossups.p: Before naming this substance, its discoverer called it “mould juice,” and he first described it in a 1929 paper. He had found it at St. Mary’s Hospital in London after returning from a summer vacation in 1928.
tossups.r: He saw that bacteria near a spot of mold on one of his dishes had been destroyed. For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: One form of this drug, labeled with the letter G, is usually given as a shot because stomach acid breaks it down, while a form labeled V can be swallowed as a pill. Amoxicillin and ampicillin are partly man-made relatives of this drug.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antibiotic, discovered when Alexander Fleming saw a mold killing bacteria.

tossups.p: This drug works best against Gram-positive bacteria, whose thick cell walls hold on to a purple stain, such as the bacteria that cause strep throat. It does nothing against viruses, so it cannot cure a cold or the flu.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antibiotic, first found in a mold by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: In his 1945 Nobel Prize lecture, this drug’s discoverer warned that using too little of it could let bacteria become resistant to it. Ernst Chain, a German-born scientist who had moved to England in 1933, helped purify this drug with the Australian Howard Florey.
tossups.r: It was first noticed when a mold killed bacteria on a lab dish. For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: Years before finding this drug, its Scottish discoverer found lysozyme [“LYE-soh-zime”], a germ-fighting enzyme in tears and mucus. That discoverer was born on a farm in Ayrshire, Scotland, and did his research at St. Mary’s Hospital in London.
tossups.r: In 1928, he noticed that a mold had killed bacteria on one of his culture plates. For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: John Sheehan of MIT first made this drug entirely from simple chemicals in 1957, though it is still mostly produced by growing mold in huge tanks. Its molecule has a four-membered beta-lactam ring joined to a five-membered ring that contains sulfur.
tossups.r: It blocks bacteria from building their cell walls. For 10 points, name this antibiotic that Alexander Fleming discovered in 1928.

tossups.p: The mold spore that led to this drug’s discovery may have drifted up from a mold research lab on the floor below its discoverer’s lab. He had left his dishes of staph bacteria stacked on a bench while he took a summer vacation.
tossups.r: When he returned in September 1928, he saw that the mold had killed bacteria near it. For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: Early supplies of this drug were so scarce that doctors at Oxford recovered it from patients’ urine to use again, since the kidneys clear it from the blood quickly. Ernst Chain and Howard Florey led the Oxford team that first tested it on people, in 1941.
tossups.r: This drug was mass-produced in the United States during World War II. For 10 points, name this antibiotic first noticed by Alexander Fleming.

tossups.p: Cephalosporins [“SEF-uh-loh-SPOR-inz”] share a four-membered beta-lactam ring with this drug, and like it, they were first found in a fungus. Both kinds of drugs kill bacteria by stopping them from building their cell walls.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming after a mold spoiled one of his dishes of bacteria.

clues.t: Discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, when a mold killed the bacteria growing near it on a dish
One of the first antibiotics, drugs that kill bacteria
Made naturally by a mold, a kind of fungus
Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in medicine for it
Works against bacteria, not viruses, so it can’t cure a cold or the flu
Fleming found it at St. Mary’s Hospital in London, after a summer vacation
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain’s team at Oxford turned it into a usable medicine in 1940–1941
Kills bacteria by stopping them from building their cell walls, so they burst
Blocks transpeptidase enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan in the bacterial wall
Human cells have no cell walls, so it leaves them unharmed
Its key structure is a strained, four-membered beta-lactam ring
Mass-produced in the United States during World War II; enough was ready to treat Allied soldiers by D-Day (1944)
Some bacteria resist it with beta-lactamase enzymes; MRSA resists its relative methicillin
Amoxicillin and ampicillin are partly man-made members of its family
Works best on Gram-positive bacteria, like the ones that cause strep throat
Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin found its structure by X-ray crystallography in 1945; she won the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
In Peoria, Illinois, “Moldy Mary” found a high-yield mold strain on a cantaloupe, and corn steep liquor in deep tanks boosted production
Norman Heatley worked out how to extract it at Oxford, where the mold grew in containers that included bedpans
In 1940, Florey and Chain showed it could protect infected mice
Fleming first called it “mould juice” and described it in a 1929 paper
Years earlier, Fleming had discovered lysozyme, a germ-fighting enzyme in tears and mucus
In 1942, Anne Miller of New Haven, Connecticut, was one of the first U.S. patients treated successfully with it
The G form is usually given as a shot because stomach acid breaks it down; the V form can be swallowed
In his 1945 Nobel lecture, Fleming warned that using too little of it could let bacteria become resistant
John Sheehan of MIT first made it from simple chemicals in 1957; its second ring has five members and contains sulfur
The kidneys clear it quickly, so early Oxford doctors recovered scarce doses from patients’ urine
The mold spore behind the discovery may have drifted up from a mold lab on the floor below Fleming’s
Cephalosporins share its beta-lactam ring, block cell walls the same way, and also come from a fungus

trap.title: Drug, mold, or scientist?
trap.body: Penicillin tossups and Alexander Fleming tossups share many clues: the moldy dish, 1928, St. Mary’s Hospital, and the 1945 Nobel Prize. The mold itself belongs to the genus Penicillium, a different answer that a question may ask for as “this genus of fungi.” Relatives such as amoxicillin and methicillin have their own names, so naming one of them won’t count.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This drug,” “this antibiotic,” or “this compound” means penicillin; “this scientist” means Fleming (or Florey or Chain); “this genus” or “this fungus” means Penicillium. Saying only “antibiotics” earns a prompt, so be ready to name the drug.
trap.line: Real answer line: Penicillin (accept penicillin G or penicillin V; prompt on antibiotics; do not accept “Penicillium”)

topics.name: Prions
topics.kicker: Misfolded proteins that spread · Cause mad cow disease and kuru
topics.briefing: Prions are the strangest infectious agents known: they have no DNA or RNA at all, just a protein folded into the wrong shape. When a prion meets a normal copy of the same protein, it makes that copy misfold too, and the slow chain reaction damages the brain, leaving tiny holes that make it look like a sponge. Prions cause mad cow disease in cattle, scrapie in sheep, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in people.
topics.answerHtml: Prions (accept prion or prion proteins; prompt on proteins or misfolded proteins; do not accept “viruses” or “viroids”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1960s, Tikvah Alper found that the agent of scrapie survived doses of radiation strong enough to destroy DNA or RNA, a hint that these agents carry no genes at all. The abnormal shape of these agents is rich in flat, folded beta sheets.
tossups.r: They are misfolded proteins, and Stanley Prusiner won a Nobel Prize for discovering them. For 10 points, name these agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: The human gene for the normal form of the protein in these agents sits on chromosome 20, and inherited changes in that gene can cause fatal familial insomnia. The “protein-only hypothesis,” championed by Stanley Prusiner, said that these agents need no genes to spread.
tossups.r: They spread by forcing normal copies of a protein to misfold. For 10 points, name these infectious agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: D. Carleton Gajdusek [“GUY-duh-shek”] shared the 1976 Nobel Prize for showing that kuru, a disease of the Fore [“FOR-ay”] people of Papua New Guinea, could be passed to chimpanzees. Kuru, whose name means “trembling,” spread through traditional funeral customs and is now known to be caused by these agents.
tossups.r: They also cause scrapie in sheep. For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins behind mad cow disease.

tossups.p: Chronic wasting disease, which affects deer, elk, and moose in North America, is caused by these agents. In sheep and goats, these agents cause scrapie, a disease named for the way sick animals rub and scrape themselves against fences.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these infectious misfolded proteins that also cause mad cow disease in cattle.

tossups.p: Some yeast cells carry versions of these agents that pass traits on to their daughter cells without any change to their DNA. Those traits are inherited through the shape of a protein rather than through genes.
tossups.r: Like the kind found in mammals, they copy themselves by making normal proteins misfold. For 10 points, name these agents, which cause mad cow disease in cattle.

tossups.p: In 1982, Stanley Prusiner coined the name of these agents by shortening the phrase “proteinaceous infectious particle,” and in 1997 he won the Nobel Prize in medicine for discovering them. Many scientists at first doubted his claim that these agents spread disease without any genes.
tossups.r: Unlike viruses, they contain no DNA or RNA. For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: In 1996, British scientists linked a new form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob [“KROITS-felt YAH-kohb”] disease in young people to eating beef from cattle sick with an illness caused by these agents. That cattle illness had spread when cows were fed meal made from the remains of infected animals.
tossups.r: These agents are proteins folded into the wrong shape. For 10 points, name these infectious agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: These agents are rich in flat beta sheets, which let them stack into long fibers called amyloid [“AM-uh-loyd”] that clump together in brain tissue. The normal version of their protein sits on the outer surface of nerve cells and is folded mostly into spiral alpha helices.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins, which have no DNA or RNA, that cause diseases such as mad cow disease.

tossups.p: Hospitals use extra-strong cleaning, such as long, very hot steam treatments or harsh chemicals, on surgical tools that might carry these agents, because ordinary sterilizing does not reliably destroy them. Cooking meat does not destroy these agents either.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins that cause mad cow disease and contain no genes.

tossups.p: Diseases caused by these agents are called transmissible spongiform encephalopathies [“en-SEF-uh-LOP-uh-theez”], because they leave tiny holes that make brain tissue look like a sponge under a microscope. Those diseases can take years or even decades to show symptoms after infection.
tossups.r: They are misfolded proteins with no DNA or RNA. For 10 points, name these agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: The abnormal form of the protein in these agents partly resists being cut apart by the enzyme proteinase K, which completely digests the normal form, even though both forms have the same sequence of amino acids. Researchers use that resistance to detect these agents in brain samples.
tossups.r: One of these agents acts as a template that makes normal copies of its protein refold into its own abnormal shape. For 10 points, name these agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: Viroids [“VYE-roydz”] are infectious agents made of nothing but a small loop of RNA, and they infect plants such as potatoes. These agents are even simpler, with no RNA or DNA at all, and antibiotics and antiviral drugs do not work against them.
tossups.r: These misfolded proteins cause scrapie in sheep. For 10 points, name these agents that cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: The misfolded form of the protein in these agents is labeled with the letters “Sc,” short for scrapie, while the healthy form is labeled with a “C,” for cellular. Scrapie, a disease of sheep and goats caused by these agents, has been known in Europe for centuries.
tossups.r: Stanley Prusiner named these agents in 1982. For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins that also cause mad cow disease.

tossups.p: The most common human disease caused by these agents, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, usually appears for no known reason in older adults, while a smaller share of cases run in families. Kuru, a disease once found among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, is caused by these agents as well.
tossups.r: They are proteins folded into the wrong shape. For 10 points, name these agents behind mad cow disease.

tossups.p: In 1988, Britain banned feeding cattle meal made from the remains of sheep and cattle, trying to stop an epidemic caused by these agents. That epidemic peaked in the early 1990s, and in 1996 the European Union banned exports of British beef.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these misfolded proteins that cause bovine spongiform encephalopathy, better known as mad cow disease.

Named by Stanley Prusiner, who won the 1997 Nobel Prize in medicine for discovering them

Cause scrapie in sheep and goats, named for how sick animals scrape against fences
Cause Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in humans
Cause kuru, a “trembling” disease of the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, spread by traditional funeral customs
Cause chronic wasting disease in deer, elk, and moose
Their diseases, transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, leave sponge-like holes in brain tissue
The name is short for “proteinaceous infectious particle,” coined in 1982

Mad cow disease spread through cattle feed made from the remains of infected animals

Their diseases can take years or even decades to show symptoms
The normal protein sits on the surface of nerve cells and is mostly alpha helices; the misfolded form is rich in beta sheets
Misfolded copies stack into long fibers called amyloid that clump in brain tissue
In the 1960s, Tikvah Alper showed the scrapie agent survives radiation strong enough to destroy DNA and RNA
D. Carleton Gajdusek shared the 1976 Nobel Prize for showing kuru could be passed to chimpanzees
The “protein-only hypothesis” says they need no genes to spread

trap.title: Agent or disease?
trap.body: Prion tossups and tossups on the diseases prions cause share almost every clue, so players blurt “mad cow disease” or “Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease” when the question wants the agent, or the reverse. Players also say “viruses,” but prions have no genes at all, and viroids are a different agent made only of RNA.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “These agents,” “these particles,” or “these proteins” means prions; “this disease” wants a disease name, like mad cow disease (BSE), scrapie, kuru, or CJD. Genes inside a protein coat mean a virus, and a bare loop of RNA means a viroid. Saying only “proteins” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Prions (accept prion proteins; prompt on proteins; do not accept “viruses”)
